                                and
                               gp.groupId IN (SELECT groupId

Q: How can I avoid redundant comparisons when checking rectangle overlaps in C#? A:

Since each node in the recursive structure will store exactly one rect.

If rectangles intersect, there will be more than 1 rectangle in the leaf (even after splitting). If you split objects into very small parts and/or store each object in its own leaf, it will be slow to search for many small objects inside a large rectangle. Usually, the leaves store several objects, and the maximum value is adjusted.

However, you are talking about the QuadTree implementation, where object(s) is(are) stored in leaves, which are accessed through nested branches. I also mentioned the QuadTree implementation, where the branches themselves can store objects. And in order to find objects, it is not necessary to look through the branches to their full depth. This approach allows you to quickly add objects without splitting into parts (imagine that you need to split a circle or a non-convex polygon), and also not to perform a rebuild, as, for example, in the R-Tree.

Q: Declaring and using a pointer is assembly A:

Sure, if you want the pointer as a global variable in static storage. (Especially for access from other functions. Or in a function other than main as a way to keep it around after the current function returns, other than making it the return value from a helper function.) Well actually since you didn't use global, it's file-scoped like a C static variable at global scope.

Your read_file function's return value is currently just the return value of close. You could return the malloced pointer in RAX. (Or 0 for error. Or even -1 .. -4095 for error codes like the Linux kernel uses, if you want to be able to signal a range of different error codes, since you use raw syscall but don't update errno. Or you could return the pointer in RAX, and success/fail status in FLAGS so the caller can jc or jnc to check for error before using RAX).

Also, of course you wouldn't free the buffer holding the file contents before returning.

Global/static variables are easy to use in asm (but less efficient than registers of course), and this is a common style for small and/or naive or at least simplistic programs since it associates names with memory locations in the source code. But global variables have all the same downsides they do in high-level languages in terms of making it easy to write spaghetti code where different functions do different things to global or static variables and it's hard to keep track of which function is responsible for what. (Not a problem in tiny programs.)

For variables used only while a certain function is running, static storage (in .bss) isn't ideal since the space is reserved for the lifetime of the program. (It's also not re-entrant in a multi-threaded program or a function that can be called from itself or from one of its children.)

A compiler would use stack space for local variables if it had to spill them from registers at all. (See How to remove "noise" from GCC/clang assembly output? for more about looking at compiler output to see how they do things.)

In asm you don't need to (and in NASM can't) "declare" local variables, you just use comments to keep track of which register (or slot of stack space) holds which high-level variable. That's the normal way to use pointers and integers. Global variables should be rare.

For example, you don't need to reload with mov rdi, [file_buffer], the pointer is still in RAX as the return value of free, so you would normally just mov rdi, rax there. (Even if you're also storing a copy of it with mov [file_buffer], rax.)

Also, I wouldn't name it file_buffer, I'd put ptr in the name like fbuff_ptr or something to record the fact that the label is attached to a qword holding a pointer, not the actual buffer itself. (It's common in simplistic asm programs to just put the whole buffer in .bss with a build-time-constant size.)

To access the pointed-to memory, you need the pointer in a register. (e.g. movzx eax, byte [rdi] or movaps [rdi], xmm0 - malloc returns 16-byte-aligned memory in the x86-64 SysV ABI since that's alignof(max_align_t)). So it normally makes the most sense to always keep it in a register in a small simple program, not reserving any memory to store the pointer itself, and not spending instructions storing/reloading them. Same as any other variable of 64-bit or less.

x86-64 has 15 GPRs not counting the stack pointer RSP so you do have lots of room in small programs / functions. But only 6 of them (RBX, RBP, R12-R15) are call-preserved in the x86-64 SysV ABI, so you can easily run out of regs that survive across function calls (e.g. to malloc and free) and may need to reserve some stack space for them. (e.g. sub rsp, 16 / add rsp, 16). Like you're using R12 to hold the file-descriptor. BTW, file-descriptors are 32-bit, so you could just do mov r12d, eax, although that doesn't help with code-size since there's a high register so it still needs a REX prefix.
